idiom_name: ScalaMock mock[T] with expects/returns (stub[T] for property-style doubles)
implementation_notes: ScalaMock works from the trait: mock[PriceService] builds a stand-in whose expectations are declared as (mock.price _).expects("A-1").returns(Money(9, 99)) and verified per test, while stub[T] records calls without ordering expectations, which suits tests that only need canned answers. In effect-style code bases the dominant seam is the environment rather than a mock object: ZIO Test supplies test implementations of services through the environment, so production logic runs against a layer whose data the test controls. ScalaMock's core module ships the stubs, and framework integrations are separate modules for scalatest, specs2, munit, ZIO and cats-effect.
pitfalls: Expectations belong to a test: a mock created in a fixture and reused carries expectations into the next test, and ScalaMock reports the mismatch against the wrong example.

Mocking a final class or a singleton object needs the dedicated object support, and on Scala 3 the macro-based module is required - a plain mock of a non-open class fails at runtime rather than at compile time.
Providing a test layer for one service in an effect system can satisfy requirements the test did not mean to fulfil, so a test can pass while the wiring it was meant to check is absent.

variants.name: ZIO Test service implementation provided through a layer
variants.implementation_notes: In ZIO the stand-in is an implementation of the service's interface provided as a layer, and the test swaps the environment: the effect system's own test services (TestConsole, TestClock, TestRandom, TestSystem) are built this way, and the same technique covers user services. This keeps the client code pure - it describes the dependency in its environment instead of holding a mock object - and determinism comes from the provided layer rather than from expectation order.
pitfalls: A layer provided once at suite level leaks state between tests; build the environment per test and keep the fake's data immutable.
Test implementations that always succeed never exercise the failure channel, so the typed error paths stay unverified.
